data.title: CORS
data.tagline: CORS is the browser security mechanism that lets a page read a cross-origin response only after the server explicitly permits it.
data.learningOutcome: You can distinguish CORS from login, tokens, and backend authorization, then check which frontend origin and request type need permission.
data.description: When a page on `app.example.com` requests `api.example.com`, the server must allow that page origin in its response before the browser gives the data to script. It protects cross-origin reads in browsers; the server still decides whether an API can be called and whether a user has permission.

learning.assumes: You have seen a page call an API on another domain or a cross-origin error in the browser console.
learning.outcome: You can distinguish CORS from login, tokens, and backend authorization, then check which frontend origin and request type need permission.

distinctions.label: Authentication
distinctions.explanation: CORS decides whether browser code may read a cross-origin response. Authentication identifies the requester, and passing both checks still does not grant business authorization.

explanation.title: An origin comes from the address
explanation.text: A different protocol, domain, or port can mean a different origin. A local page at `localhost:3000` calling `localhost:4000` is a common cross-origin case too.

explanation.title: The server declares the allowed scope
explanation.text: Before the browser exposes a response, it checks CORS response headers. A server should allow the real sites, methods, and credentials needed—not every origin just to remove an error.

data.boundary: CORS is not authentication, login, or database authorization. Even when a browser may read a response, the server must verify identity and permission. Conversely, a signed-in user can still see a CORS error when the server did not allow the current page origin.

lessonPractice.title: A local page at `localhost:3000` calls an API at `localhost:4000` and the console reports CORS. Which investigation is most accurate?

options.label: Allow `http://localhost:3000` at the API and verify the request method and credential rules
options.feedback: Correct. The two ports are different origins, and the browser needs matching permission in the API response.

options.label: Change the page request to `no-cors` and keep reading the API data in the same way
options.feedback: `no-cors` normally produces an opaque response that page script cannot read, so the original data flow still does not work.

options.label: Allow `http://localhost:4000` because that is the address receiving the request
options.feedback: CORS must allow the page origin that initiates the request, which is 3000 here; 4000 is the API destination.

data.agentPrompt: Investigate the CORS error when `http://localhost:3000` calls `http://localhost:4000`. Allow only the origin, methods, and credentials needed by this development page; do not open every origin. Then make a real browser request to verify it.
